## A. Defining Epistemology, Hermeneutics and Discourse

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GuWg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0cd3846f-a1e2-473d-8838-cab67e2bad63_1024x1536.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GuWg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0cd3846f-a1e2-473d-8838-cab67e2bad63_1024x1536.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The word darśana derives its meaning from the Sanskrit root - dṛś ‘to look at’, ‘to view’, ‘experience.’ This exposition invites contemporary scholarship to reflect on how Hindus have historically understood and interpreted their own intellectual traditions, which naturally sets it apart from other epistemological studies. As an *āstika* tradition, it reflects a community-driven theological discourse shaped by the social, psychological, and intellectual life of the religion.

With the decline of the institutions that once provided the scholarly training needed to convey a structured meaning of the Hindu canonical texts to the larger public that informed its ritualists and theists of an unbroken tradition of their theology, a rather unorthodox school of thought has entered the field. This approach is often unequipped with the textual and theological foundations of the broader tradition. As a result, it struggles to develop a justified understanding of a subject that differs significantly, in both theory and practice, from dominant Western hermeneutical traditions. A theological tradition, at its core, derives meaning from the specific terms and concepts native to its own historical discourse — terms that carry meaning only within that tradition. “Discourse is a meditation of a shareable thought, as a result, both rhetoric and hermeneutics share a common relationship of the dialectic, that is thinking embodied within the said discourse.” Reading a text is a method of relating to discourse. Religious hermeneutics — the art of interpretation — is fundamentally about understanding: one must grasp the original thought behind a discourse, because language itself inherently shapes and modifies meaning as it passes through time.

For instance, even scholars beginning their study of literature or historiography recognize that applying a foreign hermeneutical framework to a discourse outside its original context can be of limited value. This is particularly true in the case of foundational texts of the Vedanta or later puranic literature, since their *critical investigation* is guided by the organs of scriptural hermeneutics of the Hindus, namely Uttara Mīmāṃsā (for contemporary understanding). Popular canonical texts informing the absolute metaphysical realities of the hindu theology ranging from commentaries on *Itihāsa* to *smṛti* have been susceptible to misinterpretation due to the absence of a widely accessible contemporary research methodology informed by native methods of theological exegesis.

It is only reasonable that a thorough theological exegesis of the metaphysics of a religion be understood through an education that fully conveys its poetic and theistic beauty. For instance, it is advised that the texts that build upon the Bhagavat Purana expounding on the metaphorical representations of the discourse are studied strictly within the scope of the *Mīmāṁsā Shastra* that categorically informs the study within the scope of the subject. If Smriti (representing the written tradition within the religion) is the constitution of a collective civilisation consciousness, then Mīmāṁsā is the science of interpretation citing its circumstance, temperament and context integrated within.

Within the framework of the Indian Knowledge System: textual authority and legitimate modes of interpretation are constituted in disciplined auxiliary sciences known collectively as *Vedāṅgas*. These disciplines—*Śikṣā* (phonetics), *Chandas* (meter), *Vyākaraṇa* (grammar), *Nirukta* (etymology), *Kalpa* (ritual practice), and *Jyotiṣa* (astronomy)—ensure the correct recitation, interpretation, and application of Vedic knowledge.

Correct enunciation occupies a position of central importance in the Vedic tradition. While phonetics constitutes the general study of speech sounds across languages, its significance within the Vedic linguistic system is unparalleled. This is because even the slightest deviation in the vocalization of a syllable can compromise the operative potency of a mantra; in certain cases, such misarticulation may not merely nullify the intended effect but actively produce an outcome contrary to its purpose.

A study of religion removed from its original textual context, attitude and meaning is crude, unjust to the thought that is meant to be conveyed. Unlike certain strands of popular post-structuralist criticism, the author here is *not* dead but lives on through a continuing religious tradition embodied in ritual, practice, and meditation.. Whilst the existence of a liberal school of thought enables the plurality of interpretations, orthodox readers must fixate internal hermeneutic autonomy to their study bringing academic transparency to the field of their study.

## B. Contemporary *Rasa* Discourse 

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The central intervention in the study of epistemology (the study of how we know things) lies in his distinction between the conditions of cognition and the objects of cognition. Knowing subjectivity does not arise from a passive reception of reality but from the active synthesis performed by the understanding through a priori categories. These categories do not describe things as they are in themselves (noumena) rather they structure how things appear to us (phenomena) and make experiences intelligible. This distinction has important implications for literary interpretation. Conceptual frameworks do not uncover the ultimate essence of an object, instead, they shape the way that object appears to a historically situated reader or consciousness.

Although the question of how modern literary theory oversteps into the domain of other traditions’ texts *herein* is unsolicited; it is necessary to provide a rebuttal to a misaligned reading of Hinduism within the scope of traditional hermeneutics to attempt to critique the deliberate situation of the modern queer theory in the study of hindu epistemology, revisiting at first, the puranic female identity and thenceforth establishing a rigorous synchronic approach to the exclusive parables of reading *Sanskrit* and the wider vernacular. Recent post-structuralist theoretical engagements with the female identity in bhakti literature such as Bhattacharya’s (The Transgendered Devotee: Ambiguity of Gender in Devotional Poetry.) reading of Mirabai and Surdas, moves beyond conventional hetero-normative readings of 2 gender and metaphysical inquiry to assume that spiritual expressions of gender reveal alternative sexual identities. While such readings expose real weaknesses in how theory is applied, they also risk methodological overreach — a problem best addressed through a structuralist framework that validates interpretive categories drawn from within the tradition itself.

Western indology attempts to understand the constitution of gender in rasa sāstra, but *rasa sāstra* inherently extols the *anirvacanīya* (loosely comparable to the idea of a numoenon): signifying qualities that transcend the nature of definition linked to mysticism, describing experiences that defy phenomenal boundaries and embody an indistinct nature between existence and non-existence. The transcendentalism of bhakti operates within the metaphysics of self-annihilation (*ātma-laya*) over identity assertion. When Surdas speaks as a woman, or Mira imagines herself as Krishna’s bride, the gesture is ontological and not sexual; an individual engaged in the experience of *rasa* is not *becoming queer* but is engaged in the process of *unbecoming human*, transcending not merely gender but also identity, intellect and mind.

The study of the Rāsapañcādhyāyī elucidates the affirmation of a deliberate humiliation and transcendence of *kama* (eros). Kandarpa—the god of love who having subdued even the great deities such as Hari, Hara, and Brahmā, is himself overcome by Kṛṣṇa within the *rāsa-krīḍā*. This subjugation occurs through transcendence of indulgence in desire through Kṛṣṇa’s resort to “*yoga-māyām upāśritaḥ*” (having employed yoga-māyā) whereby, as the text emphasizes, “without touching the wife of another man, he enjoyed himself in his natural eternal bliss”, further affirmed through the declaration “*ātmārāmo ’pyariramat.*” Kṛṣṇa thus appears as a participant who governs kāma as *Manmatha-mathana*, the subduer of the god of love himself. The erotic register of the Rāsapañcādhyāyī functions only as an apparent pretext (upādhi), through which these five chapters guide the reader toward spiritual detachment and renunciation rather than sensual fulfillment. Śuka’s narration consistently situates *rāsa* beyond ordinary desire but within the metaphysics of self-sufficiency (*ātmarāmatva*), wherein *bhagwan* remains untouched by the very forces he appears to evoke. This interpretive position is explicitly endorsed by Dhanpata Sūri in his Bhāgavatagūḍhārthadīpikā, where he affirms Śuka’s view that the pañcādhyāyī ultimately leads to renunciation of saṃsāra. Far from encouraging identification with erotic subjectivity.

***तद्व्रजस्त्रियः श्रुत्य वेणुगीतं स्मरोदयम्।***

***काश्चित् परोक्षम् कृष्णस्य स्वसखीभ्यः अन्ववर्णयन् ॥ 3 ॥***

***तद्वर्णयितुम् आरब्धाः स्मरन्त्यः कृष्णचेषि्टतम् ।***

***नाशकन् स्मरवेगेन विक्षप्तमनसो नर ॥ 4 ॥***

Herein, *ananga-vardhanam* emerges as a translational gloss, arising from exegetical paraphrasing by commentators explaining *smara-vega*, — the force of remembrance resulting in cognitive dislocation (*vikṣipta-manasaḥ*). The word *ananga* means ‘bodiless.’ The gopis were so engrossed in his devotion that they practically forgot their identities. The language of “enhancement” belongs to later exegetical paraphrase and modern translation, not to the 3 scriptural lexeme. This forgetfulness was enhanced by listening to the flute-call that they left their work then and there and ran to him. Even exponents of madhuriya bhakti warned that the word ananga is not used in a vulgar sense: *gramya-dharma-hetu-paktra-kamamsabhava-vivaksya*: traditional exegesis explicitly frames the apparent invocation of kāma as a partial and pedagogical concession (*kāmāṁśa*), articulated within the limits of worldly dharma (*grāmya-dharma-hetu-pātra*) and intended solely as an expressive strategy (*vivakṣā*), not as an endorsement of erotic ontology.

Later Vaiṣṇava Bhāgavata traditions, emphasize the destruction of the gross body and the creation of a new one by the word *ananga*: “the bodily form indeed perishes; therefore, what arises is new”: ***aṅgaṁ tu naśyaty eva, ato nūtana utpannaḥ***. At that very moment, the body ceases to function normally due to the agitation produced by the force of *Madana*; confusion arises, and ornaments such as garlands and necklaces are displaced and worn incorrectly.” ***\[Z\]***

While reading contemporary discourses on feminism and literary theory we must attempt to trace a crucial intellectual genealogy: from the political enfranchisement of women in first-wave feminism, through the social critiques of patriarchy in second-wave feminism, to the epistemological destabilization of gender inaugurated by Judith Butler. Any critique of contemporary gender based engagements with the semantics of a text must begin by affirming this trajectory rather than collapsing it into a monolith. The early feminist movements were major theoretical enterprises that grounded struggles that secured women’s political participation, access to education, and visibility within the public sphere. These achievements are not incidental and constitute the very conditions under which women today can participate in scholarship, including the critique of religion itself.

However, the difficulty emerges when later theoretical frameworks, especially those shaped by post-structuralist tendencies: transposing wholly onto working systems that operate under radically different ontological and epistemic assumptions. While “gynocriticism” (feminist criticism centred on women’s writing) and “écriture féminine” (the idea that women’s embodied experience produces a distinct literary voice) sought to recover women’s voices and challenge patriarchal canons, they were soon criticised for essentialising gender — presuming a stable “womanly” experience or linguistic signature. Judith Butler’s intervention responds to this problem by dissolving gender into performativity, arguing that gender is not an essence but a repeated social enactment shaped by prohibition, melancholia, and normativity. This move may remain powerful within the context it addresses—namely, modern Western societies structured by heteronormative patriarchy. Yet the application of this framework to classical literature and the Indian Knowledge Systems introduces a category error. Butler’s theory presupposes a subject whose gender is produced through repression, loss, and compensatory identification. Hindu theological anthropology, by contrast, does not locate liberation in the reconfiguration of gender identity.

Contemporary queer readings of Hindu texts often interpret cross-gendered devotional voices such as male saints speaking as female lovers of God as instances of gender subversion or proto-queer subjectivity. This move mirrors Butler’s ideology wherein gender is read as performance, deviation as resistance, and ambiguity as political critique. Yet this reading remains external to the discourse it analyzes. In *bhakti*, the adoption of feminine voice is neither a critique of patriarchy nor an assertion of alternative sexual identity; it is a rhetorical and ontological strategy rooted in *rasa* theory, where all worldly identities (including masculinity and femininity) are subordinated to a subliminal experience. Here, the distinction between political feminism and cultural anthropology becomes crucial. The early waves of feminism rightly challenged women’s exclusion from civic, educational, and literary institutions but when theory moves from critiquing social inequality to redefining the metaphysical meaning of cultural symbols, it risks overriding indigenous categories of interpretation. The discourse on Butler underscores that gender performativity leaves no space for a subject outside discourse. Hindu theology, however, precisely posits such a space: the self that is not reducible to body, sexuality, or social role. To read bhakti’s gender fluidity as performative identity rather than as intentional self-effacement is to misrecognize the telos of the tradition. In this sense, this critique calls for hermeneutic restraint and epistemic humility recognizing that not all discourses of gender are about identity politics, and not all ambiguities signal resistance.

**Nimai Verma studies English at Delhi University and works in Classics, Semantics, Philology, Comparative Linguistics and Postcolonial Studies.**
